posts.quote: MOM TESTED THE BATHWATER WITH HER ELBOW, AND THAT WAS THE ONLY THERMOMETER THE HOUSE EVER NEEDED.
posts.caption: Saturday night was bath night, and the whole routine ran like a railroad schedule. Mom turned the faucet, swirled her hand through the water, and then dipped her elbow in like she was reading a dial. Too hot, add cold. Too cold, add hot, and you stood there shivering in a towel while she decided. She had never owned a thermometer and she had never once been wrong. You got in, the water was exactly right, and a bar of soap and a washcloth with a hole in it did the rest.
posts.first: My mother tested everything with her elbow, the baby bottle, the iron, the bath. I asked her once where she learned it and she said her mother, and her mother before that. I tried it on my own kids and I think I still get it wrong, but I keep trying.

posts.quote: THE TV DINNER HAD FOUR COMPARTMENTS, ONE FOIL TRAY, AND A DESSERT THAT TOUCHED EVERYTHING.
posts.caption: Friday night meant the folding tray tables came out of the hall closet and everybody got a spot facing the television. The foil tray came out of the oven hot enough to take a fingerprint with it. Salisbury steak on one side, whipped potatoes in the middle, peas that had gone a shade too bright. And the little cobbler in the corner always bled straight into the potatoes, so you ate a bite of both and called it a combination. Nobody complained. The best seat in the house was the one closest to the set.
posts.first: The first time Mom brought one home from the grocer's, we all stood around the oven like it was a science experiment. Dad said it was the future. He ate two of them that night and went back to meat loaf by Sunday.

posts.character: Cars and driving culture (license plate game)
posts.quote: WE PLAYED THE LICENSE PLATE GAME FOR SIX HUNDRED MILES, AND DAD STILL SAID WE'D BE THERE IN AN HOUR.
posts.caption: By the time you crossed the state line, you had found Ohio, Indiana, and a mystery plate nobody could agree on. The back seat had been divided into two countries with an invisible border down the middle. Mom handed crackers over her shoulder without ever turning around. Somebody held the road atlas and swore they knew exactly where we were. And every forty minutes, like clockwork, Dad said we were about an hour away.
posts.first: Our family never made a trip without a big argument about who spotted Nevada first. I still say it was me, and my brother still says it was him. Dad kept driving and pretended he didn't hear us.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (porch entertainment)
posts.quote: Our whole entertainment system was a radio, a deck of cards, and a front porch, and nobody ever said they were bored.
posts.first: We had a deck of cards missing the seven of clubs and we played with it for years. Grandpa just wrote a seven on a piece of paper and nobody argued. Best summers of my life were on that porch.

posts.quote: RECESS / THIRTY MINUTES, ONE RUBBER BALL, AND NOBODY NEEDED A REFEREE
posts.caption: The bell rang and thirty kids hit the doors like water through a broken dam. Somebody always had the red rubber ball, and that kid got to pick the game. Kickball, tag, jump rope, marbles in the dirt by the fence. Arguments settled themselves in about nine seconds, usually with the loudest voice winning. You came back in sweaty and pink-cheeked, and the teacher gave you a look that said she remembered doing the same.
posts.first: Our schoolyard had one tall oak at the edge of the blacktop, and whoever touched it first was safe. I must have worn a path to that tree. I scraped both knees on it in third grade and I'd go back and do it again.

posts.quote: MOM DARNED SOCKS UNDER THE LAMP, AND NOTHING WE OWNED WAS THROWN AWAY UNTIL IT WAS MORE PATCH THAN SHIRT.
posts.caption: After supper, once the dishes were done, Mom settled into her chair beside the lamp with a wooden egg and a needle. A sock with a hole in the heel went over the egg, and she wove the thread back and forth like she was building a tiny fence. Nobody threw out a sock for a hole, or a shirt for a torn elbow, or a coat that had been passed down three times. A good patch was a sign of a careful house. You learned that waste was a kind of embarrassment.
posts.first: My mother kept a coffee can full of buttons from shirts that had worn out years ago. When one fell off something of mine, she'd dig through it and always find a match. I have that can now, and I can't make myself throw out a single button.

posts.quote: A STACK OF 45S, ONE RECORD PLAYER, AND A WHOLE SUMMER OF DANCING IN THE LIVING ROOM.
posts.caption: The record player lived on a card table in the corner, and the 45s lived in a shoebox beside it. You had to drop the little yellow plastic adapter into the middle or the record wouldn't sit right. The needle crackled a second before the song started, and everyone in the house knew that crackle meant good news. Somebody pushed the couch back, and the rug became a dance floor. Mom could jitterbug. Dad pretended he couldn't.
posts.first: We wore out our favorite 45 so badly it skipped in the same spot every time. We learned to sing the skip. Even now when I hear that song, I sing it the broken way.

posts.quote: WHEN A NEIGHBOR'S BARN BURNED DOWN, THE WHOLE TOWN SHOWED UP WITH HAMMERS BEFORE THE ASHES WERE COLD.
posts.caption: Nobody held a meeting about it. Somebody saw the smoke, somebody rang a bell, and by suppertime the trucks started rolling in. Men brought saws and ladders, and women brought pies and coffee in big enamel pots. The kids carried nails in coffee cans and felt important about it. By Sunday a new frame stood where the old barn had been. Nobody said thank you much, because nobody expected to be thanked.
posts.first: When I was ten, our neighbor's barn went up one August night. I remember my father taking his hammer off the nail in the garage without a word. He came home after dark with a splinter in his thumb and a smile I didn't see often.

posts.quote: What was the one room in the house you were never, ever allowed to play in?
posts.first: Ours was the front parlor, with the plastic-covered sofa and the glass candy dish nobody was allowed to touch. We were only allowed in at Christmas and when the preacher visited. I'm sixty-eight and I still tiptoe in a room like that.

posts.quote: THE PAPERBOY / FOLD IT, ROLL IT, AND THROW IT ON THE PORCH FROM A MOVING BIKE
posts.caption: He was up before the roosters with a canvas bag slung across his shoulder and a stack of papers that weighed nearly as much as he did. Fold, roll, snap the rubber band, and throw. The good ones landed on the porch mat, and the bad ones landed in Mrs. Henderson's rosebush. On collection day he knocked on every door with a little card and a pencil. The tips, a nickel here and a quarter there, paid for his first bicycle.
posts.first: I had the morning route when I was twelve. My arm got good enough that I could hit a screen door from across the street. I earned eleven dollars a week and felt like a banker.
